#8992. 5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

Strength training becomes even more critical as you age. Here’s how to do it.

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts showed significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”

Julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she says, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Cyclists who are entirely new to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue says. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

This workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural issues, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

Lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue says.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

Stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

If you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

#8991. 10-Minute Morning Yoga Routine to Wake Up Your Entire Body

This quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need. Rather than holding poses for an extended period of time, you’re moving with your breath in a fluid and rhythmic 10-minute yoga routine that will definitely energize you and target your back, hips, and hamstrings.

So if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body. I encourage you to choose a one-word intention for your day that you pause and focus on at the outset and throughout your practice. What is one word that captures how you want to feel today, what you want to focus on, or what matters to you right now?

No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.

You’re going to start by targeting the spine. From your hands and knees, your palms go underneath your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. As you inhale, lower your belly, lift your gaze and arch your back in Cow Pose.

As you exhale, reverse that motion. Thinking of pushing into your fingertips and knuckles, pushing the mat away from you, and letting your head release and your neck relax in Cat Pose.

And then go in between these two poses, getting into all parts of the spine, including the neck, upper back, mid back, lower back, all the way to your tailbone, trying to get that full range of motion.

Come back to hands and knees with a neutral spine.

Still on your hands and knees, lift your right leg and trace some circles with it, as big as you can, and then let’s reverse the direction of those circles. You’re simply trying to create movement through your right hip. You don’t need to overthink this one.

Step your right foot straight out to the side and press the outer edge of your foot against the floor. Lift yourself upright and reach your left arm overhead and toward the right in a side body stretch known as Gate Pose.

Come back to your hands and knees, tuck your toes, and hover your knees a little above the mat. You can probably feel your core engage.

Walk your feet back to keep your shoulders over your wrists in Plank Pose. Strongly press the mat away from you, drawing your lower belly inward and broadening through your upper back. Think of lengthening your tailbone toward your heels and drawing your lower belly inward and upward.

Let’s find Downward-Facing Dog. Lift your hips up and back, and peddle out your feet by straightening one leg and bending the other to stretch your ankles and calves. Keep your arms straight without locking your elbows. Feel the length through your spine.

Lower your knees to the mat and repeat the poses on your left side, including Hip Circles, Gate Pose, Hovering Tabletop, Plank, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward-Facing Dog, reach your right leg toward the sky, bend your right knee, open your hip, and take one more of those big hip circles from your Three-Legged Dog.

From Down Dog, inhale as you step your right foot forward, spin your back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat as if you were coming into Warrior 2. Exhale as you flow into Extended Side Angle, bringing your right forearm onto your right thigh and reaching your left arm overhead.

As you inhale, straighten your front leg and reach your right arm all the way back in Reverse Triangle.

Then exhale back into Extended Side Angle, sinking your hips a little lower. Repeat that flow twice more like this.

Bring both palms to the mat on either side of your right foot and find Pigeon Pose from here. So take your right knee behind your right wrist and reach your left leg straight back. Inhale as you come high onto your fingertips to lift and lengthen, then exhale as you bend forward.

Move in between the two shapes twice more as you undulate through the spine. Then the next time you lower yourself close to the mat, stay here for 5 long, slow breaths. Try to release tension through your shoulder blades and arms.

When you’re ready, lift yourself off the mat and find your Downward-Facing Dog. If you like, you can first come forward into Plank and then lower yourself to the mat and take Cobra. Then repeat these poses on your left side, starting with Three-Legged Dog, Dynamic Extended Side Angle, and Dynamic Pigeon.

Come back to Downward-Facing Dog. Pause here for several breaths.

Bring your knees to the mat and take a seat. As with most morning practices, I don’t include a Savasana in case you might be tempted to fall back asleep, but you’re always welcome to take it on your own.

Sit tall and roll your shoulders down and away from your ears. Maybe you bring your hands together at the front of your heart. Pause here for as long as you can.

Thank you so much for doing this quick vinyasa flow at home with me. May you feel really good and have gotten a boost of energy. Let me know what your intention is for the day ahead in a comment below.

#8990. 7 Common 5K Training Mistakes Runners Make

Everything you should avoid for a faster 3.1 miles.

The 5K is a staple in many runners’ racing schedules, and training for one comes with its own unique strategies for interval workouts, long runs, nutrition, and recovery. All of these factors are bound to leave room for error, so you’ll likely run into some pitfalls as you prep for 3.1 miles.

Some common missteps runners face might even lead to injury, explains Maya Ellison, C.P.T., RRCA-certified run coach and owner of P.A.C.E.D. Coaching Services. If you don’t optimize your training method, you’re also likely to keep getting the same results, which may not lead to that PR you’re vying to achieve, she says. Even if you’re a seasoned runner with dozens of 5Ks under your belt, there’s always room for improvement. “Doing it before doesn’t make you an expert,” says Ellison.

So you can surely take a couple notes from run coaches in order to run your best 5K yet. To better prepare for all your favorite seasonal 3.1-milers and help you feel confident at the start line, we spoke with run coaches to unpack the most common mistakes runners make when training for a 5K.

For many runners, 5Ks are easier to jump into compared to a marathon, which requires a solid block of training time to adjust to high mileage and fueling demands. With a 5K, you might tag along at a friend’s race or sign up last minute. Because of this, you might squeeze in a bunch of speed workouts within a few weeks before the race, which can leave you feeling tired or flat come race day, says Sam Renikoff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach.

While you can get away with a shorter training block for a 5K, it’s still important to give yourself enough time to absorb your training, recover, and feel 100 percent going into the race, Renikoff explains. For example, rather than tapering for three weeks before race day like you would training for a marathon, Renikoff recommends tapering for a week to 10 days before a 5K, keeping intensity high with speedwork but cutting back on volume.

Plus, going from zero to 100 can lead to getting sidelined, according to Debbie Woodruff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach and certified personal trainer. That’s because runners who increase mileage too quickly—rather than taking small steps toward more volume—are more likely to face injury, according to a study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.

To mitigate the risk, Woodruff recommends beginners follow a couch-to-5K plan or a run/walk training plan to ease into training with a gradual buildup, while more seasoned runners should follow an eight-week-long plan that also allows you to build mileage, add speedwork, and prioritize the prerace taper.

Sticking to an expert-backed training plan, like Runner’s World’s 5K training plans, allows you to have structure and give yourself time to adjust to the demands of the distance.

Renikoff explains that even though 5Ks are much shorter than a marathon or half, the long run is still crucial. It allows you to get comfortable with being uncomfortable, an important part of the 5K. It also prevents you from giving into fatigue by building your endurance, which allows you to hold onto your pace through the entire 3.1 miles. Plus, the long run often acts as a confidence booster, making the 5K less intimidating all around.

The long run is one of the best ways to increase your aerobic capacity, Renikoff explains. This is important even for shorter race distances because you need to use oxygen to efficiently produce energy for any run lasting longer than just a few minutes.

Long runs during 5K training will typically range anywhere from 4.5 miles (for more beginners) to 12 miles (for advanced runners with time-based goals like breaking 20 minutes). That means some plans may triple the distance of your race, which will only make you more prepared to conquer 3.1 miles.

Seasoned runners in particular might struggle to keep their easy runs easy, Ellison explains, because of their experience, fitness levels, or overall ambition. But these easy days give your body a chance to recover from hard days, allowing you to get stronger throughout your training cycle, she says.

You should feel relaxed throughout your easy runs, like you’re able to have a conversation with someone. Some runners find it helpful to check in on their effort level with the ABC test: Chant the ABCs out loud and try to get to the letter G without having to take a breath. If you falter, that’s your cue that you need to slow down.

If you make a habit of not taking easy pace seriously, you might even find yourself running a speedy first mile during an easy run or tempo run, only to falter by mile two, progressively getting slower and more fatigued by the end. This happens when runners struggle to find an effective pacing strategy, Renikoff explains.

This makes it more likely you’ll go out too fast on race day, which could sabotage your goals. “If you go out and run the first mile [of the race] 20 seconds faster than your average 5K pace, you’re a lot more likely to have that pace balloon to 30 seconds or more slower [than goal pace] in the second and third miles, which is not only not fun or enjoyable, but it’s also not fast,” Renikoff says.

For smarter pacing, Renikoff suggests progression runs: Start by running the first mile of your tempo run at a moderate pace, then increase your speed each mile or half mile (depending on the distance of your run) by about 10 seconds, finishing significantly faster than you started. This requires you to start slow enough that you can continue to run faster as the workout progresses.

While some runners start their runs too fast, others struggle to run faster than their easy pace at all. “If you’re aiming to run a fast 5K and you have not spent any time in those paces by doing some hard intervals, it’s really easy to give up in the race,” says Renikoff.

The key to not giving up at the first sign of fatigue? Implement one to two days per week of some form of speed training, including intervals and tempo runs, Woodruff says.

Seasoned runners may benefit from track intervals, like 200- to 400-meter repeats at 95-percent effort or goal 5K pace with equal recovery, she explains. Another option is a tempo or threshold run, where you sustain your 5K pace for a prolonged period of time sandwiched by a few easy miles.

A fartlek workout introduces newbie runners to interval training, Woodruff explains, by alternating one to two minutes at a hard effort with one to two minutes at an easy effort, essentially practicing interval training without the need for specific metrics.

If your most recent PR is a 24-minute 5K and you’re trying to run your next one in 19 minutes, you might need to readjust your goal setting, at least for now. Ellison explains that runners sometimes set overly ambitious goals, when in reality, true growth takes time.

Instead of looking to drop five minutes in your next race—which requires you to run nearly two minutes faster per mile—try setting a smaller goal like dropping 30 seconds to one minute from your finish time, Ellison explains. This requires about a 10- to 20-second pace difference per mile, making your PR more manageable to achieve.

A beginner 5K runner may not know how to properly warm up and cool down, explains Ellison, which is especially important for each workout, but also for race day.

Warmups can help you sustain a harder effort for longer periods of time, while cooldowns give your body a chance to actively recover after hard efforts. A solid warmup typically includes dynamic stretching, drills like high knees and butt kicks, along with a five-minute jog, Woodruff explains, while a cooldown should include a mile or two of easy jogging and static stretching.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

JAL's inflight service is consistently ranked among the best in the world. The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. On a US-to-Japan routing, you could stop in Tokyo for four or five days, then continue to Osaka or another Japanese city (on a separate ticket), effectively getting a multi-city Japan trip from a single 60,000-mile award. Discuss this with the Alaska agent when booking.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles. Stack two cardholders in your household — you and your partner each earn a welcome bonus — and you have a round-trip business class redemption funded almost entirely from sign-up offers.

Marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

While JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, New Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

Alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

This redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. If Japan is on your bucket list and you're willing to do a phone call to complete the booking, this is one of the highest-value redemptions in the entire loyalty ecosystem.

Minimum points needed: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. A couple needs 120,000 miles for two one-way Business Class tickets.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — and that rating is honest. It's not beginner-friendly (rated 2 out of 5 for beginners), but it's absolutely achievable for anyone willing to learn the two-step process. **What makes it moderate:** First, earning Alaska miles is less straightforward than earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex points. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Plan. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The booking becomes a five-minute transaction. 3. **Book 6–10 months out** for peak dates — this eliminates most of the availability stress and gives you time to transfer points if needed. If you've already booked one partner award by phone with any airline, this will feel familiar. If this is your first, the effort is absolutely worth it for a redemption worth 8–17 cents per point.

No. Alaska Mileage Plan is not a transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards. Your primary earning paths are the Alaska Airlines credit card, Marriott Bonvoy transfers, and purchasing miles during Alaska's periodic sales.

No. JAL flights booked with Alaska miles do not carry fuel surcharges. You will pay only government taxes and fees, typically $25-$50 for a one-way transpacific ticket. This is a major advantage over booking through some other programs.

The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.

#8988. What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

Who holds the Ironman world record? Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time. (Photo: Ironman (Donald Miralle), Challenge Family, FinisherPix)

After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.

That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024

And yet, despite all these amazing feats, there are no world records in full-distance racing.

Confused? It’s understandable. Pour yourself a cup of coffee and get ready to learn why Ironman (and iron-distance) world records technically don’t exist.

In the world of running, 26.2-mile marathons must adhere to rigorous certification standards set by World Athletics that include restrictions on things like point-to-point courses, elevation drop, and (recent) International measurement, but triathlon operates without such official oversight. Course configurations are notoriously inconsistent, often shifting from one season to the next, and triathletes don’t even think twice about point-to-point courses or elevation drops between start and finish.

Certainly course distances are confirmed in high-level World Triathlon races like the Olympics, but there is no course certification for long-course or for regular age-group races. Often, you’ll hear athletes remark that their GPS watch clocked an Ironman course as short or long – rarely does a race hit exactly 2.4 miles of swimming, 112 miles of cycling, and 26.2 miles of running. Those are ballpark figures that races would love to hit if they can, but permitting issues might mean the host city can only close 110 miles of roads for the bike course – this occurred at Ironman Texas in 2018, when “Ironman record times” were clocked by Melissa Hauschildt and Matt Hanson.

Beyond the logistics, an athlete’s clock is at the mercy of Mother Nature; factors like local climate, hilly terrain, or even a current-assisted swim can skew the data (as was the case in 2021, when Blummenfelt floated downcurrent to a 39:41 swim en route to a then “Ironman record” of 7:21:12 in Cozumel).

Because of that, Ironman confirmed in 2026 that they do not keep track of “official” world records for that reason, with a spokesperson telling Triathlete, “Due to variance of courses (even from year-to-year the same race could have course alterations), combined with the fact that unlike marathons, triathlon does not have official course certification for records, we use world best, course best, race best, swim/bike/run course best, etc.”

The same holds true for Ironman 70.3 races and non-branded half-iron triathlons; no course certification, no “official” record.

For what it’s worth, the Guinness World Records recognizes the “fastest time to complete an Ironman triathlon,” but not fastest iron-distance time (which we’ll explain in the next section). This may be more a function of marketing, as Ironman has established its own “partner” page on the Guinness Book of World Records website. Guinness does recognize some other triathlon records, including “fastest lumberjack triathlon,” which raises many other questions we’ll save for a different article.

Then there’s the branding gymnastics of Ironman™ versus an iron-distance race like Challenge Roth.

You see, even though Challenge Roth is a 140.6-mile triathlon, it’s not an Ironman. Ironman is a distinct brand of 140.6-mile races, though many use the name to designate the distance (similar to how most Americans say “pass me a Kleenex” for tissue, or “I need a Band-Aid,” instead of requesting an adhesive bandage).

And though Challenge Roth has been around for decades, the course and race have evolved. In 2010, the Challenge Roth run course was adjusted to be more spectator-friendly, and the bike course has been altered several times for safety, most recently in 2024. In 2026, Roth expanded the pro bike drafting zone from 12 to 20 meters, creating entirely different race dynamics altogether.

Ultimately, establishing a definitive “record” is difficult even for a single event, given how much can change from one year to the next. And though iron-distance “records” are often broken at Challenge Roth, they’re technically not the site of “the fastest iron-distance times in history.”

In 2022, Kristian Blummenfelt and Kat Matthews covered the 140.6-mile distance in what would have been record-setting times of 6:44:25 and 7:31:54 – except that they did it in a unique setup involving pacers, drafting, and extra equipment as part of the Sub7/Sub8 Project. The event allowed for advanced technological and athletic optimizations, featuring specialized gear like prototype bikes and pace teams on the swim and bike to provide slipstreams for Blummenfelt and Matthews to draft off of — all things you’d never be allowed to do in a legitimate race

This format drew considerable criticism and debate on social media, with the community questioning whether the Sub7/Sub8 times should be viewed as legitimate records. Many referenced Jan Frodeno’s 7:27:53 time for a similar iron-distance experiment known as Tri Battle Royle, which was held on a highly modified course featuring special ramps and a perfectly mapped swim line to remove tricky turns.

Because these events were so heavily optimized, no one regards these times as actual world records — just like the much-hyped 2017 Breaking2 Nike marketing event for the marathon record. Instead, they’re chalked up to fascinating experiments for fans to geek out over. (And for that, we’re thankful.)

So now that we’ve determined there is no official world record for Ironman, iron-distance triathlon, or otherwise, we can establish there are fastest-known times, with all the caveats above.

#8987. The Top 11 Women’s Running Shoes That Have the Comfiest Fit, Coziest Cushioning, and Most Responsive Ride

These are the current road and trail favorites of our women’s wear-test team.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 12, 2026: End-of-year sales have already taken off. Our Best Stability Shoe, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is now on sale with 19% off. (We are currently testing the newest model, the Adrenaline GTS 26.) Our Best for Speedwork Shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is also discounted with 20% off.

We are in a new era of running shoes, from stacked super trainers to plated racers to gravel models decked out with bike-inspired treads.

The industry formerly criticized for “shrink it and pink it,” i.e., the practice of making smaller-size men’s shoes and slapping pink on them and calling them women’s shoes, has gone to great lengths crafting footwear that’s women-specific.

Brands are taking care to produce shoes that accommodate the average woman’s foot shape: wider in the midfoot area, narrower around the heel. But don’t think this list is free of pink shoes. The traditionally feminine colors have been reclaimed by brands like Nike (turns out it’s flashy and easier to spot neon pink Alphaflys). Here you’ll find trainers of every color for all types of women’s feet and women runners.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Glycerin 23On a budget → New Balance EllipseMostly a run/walker → Hoka Clifton 11On the path to recovery → Hoka Bondi 9Adding in speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLLogging long runs → Nike Vomero 18Racing a marathon → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3An overpronator → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25Suffering from bunions → Altra Torin 9Running on rail trails → lululemon WildfeelNew to technical terrain → Altra Experience Wild 3

Runner’s World has been around for almost 60 years, providing news, fitness tips, and, of course, gear recommendations for runners. Our product guides for essentials like running shoes and shorts come from our hardworking test team, who put the latest and greatest running gear through their paces day in and day out. These selections come from Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen, who blazes the trails and is an ultramarathon beast, and me, Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer. I have written about running gear for a decade and hold an even longer Boston Marathon streak, beginning in 2013.

We picked these shoes based on feedback from the runners who are part of our 300-runner-strong team of local wear-testers and the expertise of our editors. We evaluated every shoe over the course of at least 100 miles, paying attention to overall performance, comfort, ride, longevity, and value.

To ensure our shoe recommendations are truly comprehensive and trustworthy, we grabbed a wide array of shoe types to put through our rigorous testing. This involved evaluating them across diverse terrains, including challenging trails, smooth tracks, varied road surfaces, and—of course—treadmills. Our massive wear-test team allows us to gather feedback from individuals ranging from sprinters to marathoners, runners of different weights and body types, those with different foot strikes, shoe needs, and biomechanics. By combining varied surface testing with a diverse runner pool, we learn a ton about each shoe’s performance and suitability for a wide range of users and individual experiences. Based on our extensive testing, the options below are currently the best running shoes for women.

In our testing, we found the Glycerin 23 excelled as a daily trainer over the Ghost 18 among women testers. The formerly max-cushioned Glycerin has evolved into an everyday shoe that you can take out on easy days to long runs. Our women testers preferred the Glycerin 23 over the Ghost 18 because of the shoes’ fit. Several testers reported hot spots in the Ghost 18’s bunion-prone area. The Glycerin 23, on the other hand, was praised for its broad platform, soft and plush knit upper, and ample wiggle room in the toebox.

“The shoe is cushioned in a way that makes me want to do all my long runs in them,” said tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “It doesn’t drag as some cushioned shoes do, but feels responsive. My go-to comparison of a cushioned shoe is the Saucony Echelon which I love for walking/hiking, but which I cannot do long miles in because the shoe drags, makes me work too hard. In comparison, the Glycerin is plushy but responds well to my moods and the corresponding pace changes.”

The shoe has Brooks’s DNA Tuned midsole foam, which was introduced in the even cushier Glycerin Max. The experience running on DNA Tuned is just like Černá described: plush, supportive, responsive, ideal for running long.

One of our women testers described the Ellipse v1 as “nearly perfect.”

New Balance’s intent with the shoe was to provide a high-cushioned, trampoline-like bounce experience for recreation. It’s the kind of shoe you can wear for daily training, while you lace up in it for a casual, conversationally paced group run. The Ellipse was specifically made to make runs easier.

Fresh Foam X is dialed in to produce a foamy, high-rebound ride with reliable shock absorption. It’s a ride that makes me look forward to lacing up the Ellipse and taking it out for whatever kind of run my heart desires on the spot. The tweaked foam makes running in the soft, springy shoe feel like a treat.

“The best word to describe the cushion is plush,” said tester Laura Parks. “It has the extreme cushion sensation of a Hoka Bondi without feeling the weight.” She described the ride as unlike any she’s had running in other Fresh Foam X models.

We’re still in the process of testing the Clifton 11, but the team is already loving the shoe weeks into testing. Everything we love about Hoka—plush cushioning, cozy fit, responsive midsole—is usually encapsulated in each iteration of the Clifton. The 11 is no exception. It was a hard follow after the ClifTEN, but the Clifton 11 makes runs feel effortless, thanks to the compression-molded EVA midsole foam, which provides high rebound and a comfy platform that pillows your foot.

The shoe has Hoka’s Meta-Rocker geometry to promote smooth transitions. Sidewalls make the fit snug but not too narrow as the Hoka Bondi 9.

The Clifton 11 is also excellent for run/walking because of that cushioned support and rocker geometry. These elements make the Clifton reliable at any pace.

The Bondi 9, one of Hoka’s plushest daily trainers, is somehow cushier and sleeker with this update. Hoka added 10 mm to the midsole—but this shoe is no chonk. We even tested it sprinting on the treadmill; the supercritically foamed EVA provides high energy return and soft support. But we especially like using the shoe for run/walking and recovery.

“The Bondi 9 delivers great protection with an amazingly smooth roll,” said tester Tiffany Volpe. “I can see why there is so much hype behind the Hoka and [why it’s called] the Queen of Cushion. I felt like I was sitting down in the midsole. I felt locked in with ample protection especially in the tongue and collar.

“I found the Bondi a perfect recovery day shoe and one that I reach for when I just want to head out for a long slow run to clear my head.”

The shoe was also rated high in stability among testers, and they appreciated the reflective, as well.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate boldly dubbed the Adizero Evo SL Shoe of the Year merely a month into 2025. That sentiment is upheld and shared; the shoe is Best Overall on our list of Best Running Shoes. For $150 (and frequently on sale), just above the cost of the New Balance Ellipse, you could also say it’s Best Value. And because of its secret sauce, Adidas’s Lightstrike Pro midsole, which is featured in the brand’s super shoes, you could also say it’s Best for Speedwork, too.

One woman tester gamely raced in the Adizero Evo SL, and experienced excellent results. “The coolest thing about these to me was the weight and cushion,” said that tester, Caroline Lennon. “It was a perfect balance of being light and springy but still feeling well-cushioned and supported. They were so comfortable at all paces and let me feel faster than I was anticipating. They felt best at a harder effort. My 5K race was surprisingly fast given that there was no carbon plate!”

Breaking: A Nike shoe with Hoka-plush cushioning. The Vomero 18 is unlike any Nike we’ve tested. It has a dual-density midsole with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foam, which puts this shoe in the super trainer category. What you get is a bouncy, soft ride that makes long runs an energized quest instead of a Saturday (or Sunday) morning slog.

“I didn’t expect to love this shoe as much as I do!” said Associate Health and Fitness Editor Kristine Kearns, a self-described loyal Brooks Ghost fan. “I wasn’t sure if I would like the Vomero 18 because of how much heel cushioning there is, and how it kind of elevates me forward in that way. But it turns out the shoe provides so much stability, even on the side.”

The source of the stability Kearns is referring to: the wider platform. Nike collected input from women testers, who wanted a wider fit in the midfoot. The result is a more accommodating foot shape that provides midrun support.

The Endorphin Elite 3 makes good with super adjustments after a strong reception with the Endorphin Elite 2. Several testers loved the previous model’s aggressive bounce, becoming inspired to race in it at their next marathon. Others, like me, had difficulty troubleshooting the squishy TPEE foam. It was volatile, pogo stick-like bounce that required mastering before you went all out on this somewhat unstable super shoe.

Saucony tamed the shoe this go-around. That pogo stick bounce is still there, but the ride is more stable with a connected heel and midfoot (not the slightly decoupled heel that made it more likely to turn your foot inward navigating sharp turns). The PwrTrac outsole also adds more support by providing grippy traction.

The Adrenaline GTS 25 is pumped with even more foam for a comfier, more supportive ride. Brooks added 1 mm of DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and 3 mm in the forefoot, resulting in a slightly higher stack height, lower heel drop, and more responsive ride.

Dense guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to help with ankle and knee alignment while running. The support aids overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

“One of the shoe’s best features is the sense of security it provides,” said tester Kylie Rodriguez. “The Adrenaline series is known for its stability, and this model is no exception. I felt confident and secure on every surface, from slick sidewalks to uneven dirt paths.

“This blend of comfort, stability, and a lightweight feel makes the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 a fantastic and reliable choice for any runner looking for a do-it-all shoe. It’s a solid, dependable performer that won’t let you down. Another solid key component to the shoe was the cupping support the heel gave my strong heel striking steps even more confidence and support.”

We’re still getting in Torin 9 feedback, but it’s safe to say early on that the shoe is a worthy follow-up to the Torin 8. When Altra was founded in 2009, its core values were balanced zero-drop cushioning, an accommodating toebox for toe-splaying, and a women-specific fit. The brand has evolved with a 4mm-drop shoe line but its values haven’t changed.

The Torin, basically the Ghost version of a zero-drop shoe, is a terrific cushioned entry into running a no-drop shoe. Dual-density foam provides a moderate but supportive bed of cushioning to help you transition into zero-drop running. Runners with wide feet and bunions will also appreciate Altra’s wide toebox, which not only allows your toes to wiggle but also helps with your biomechanics (squeezed toes help you run faster, said no one ever).

The updated outsole is Vibram XS Dura, which is grippier than the rubber on the Torin 8. I like how the shoe can dabble off road and not have to worry about falling face-first when I traverse onto a trail—which is rare.

The lululemon shoe team has made it its mission to produce women-specific trainers since the release of the brand’s first running shoe, the Blissfeel, in 2022. Their latest model, the Wildfeel, provides the same comfy, secure fit with a responsive, high-rebound ride off-road.

The shoe has men’s and women’s editions, which are tweaked to support each sex’s anatomical differences and distinct biomechanics. For instance, the forefoot of the women’s shoe is slightly more flexible than the men’s to complement the shorter toes, longer arch, and shorter instep typical of women’s feet.

Our testers appreciated the Wildfeel’s flexibility and overall comfort. It’s a good choice for runners new to the trail who want more of a hybrid option that can take on some technical track.

“I loved the flexibility of the Wildfeels!” said tester Jenny Stump. “I am primarily a road runner. These felt comfortable enough that I could do some easy miles on the road as well as tackle some trails with uneven surfaces. All the trail runners I have previously tried felt more stiff and had such a thick sole that I wouldn’t even want to warm up on the road with them.”

What I love most about the Experience Wild 3 is that it’s a trail shoe that feels like a road shoe. The fit is accommodating in the midfoot and toe area—Altra is known for its spacious toeboxes that allow your toes to splay—and the collar and tongue are padded and cushioned.

The Altra Ego P35 foam is responsive on the trail and provides a nice balance of support and ground feel. Another win for me, the mostly road runner: the shoe is incredibly flexible. No stiffness or hot spots that cause my feet a world of hurt the first couple of runs before they’re broken in.

The shoes have gaiter attachments to provide even more protection and a toe sweep. The drop is a low 4 mm, which isn’t as intimidating as going full zero (though if you’re game, the Lone Peak 9 is a good place to start).

The shoe is also available as the Experience Wild 3+, which has a Vibram Megagrip outsole. It’s a little more expensive at $165. If you want tackier grip, go for it. But the 3.5mm lugs on the MaxTrac outsole suit me and fellow testers just fine on slush, mud, and icy snow.

Women’s feet have distinct structural differences than men’s feet. From shape to proportions to biomechanics, all of these things significantly impact shoe fit and comfort. For example, while men’s feet typically present a more uniform width from heel to forefoot, women’s feet tend to be wider in the forefoot relative to the heel. Any lady who has felt their toes get squished as their heel slips right out of the shoe knows this issue.

Recognizing these anatomical differences, and responding to the hoards of women runners clamoring for something better, running shoe manufacturers have (finally) started to incorporate more gender-specific design elements into their products. This means crafting shoes with distinct features tailored to the unique shape and biomechanics of women’s feet. For instance, a women’s running shoe might feature a wider toebox to accommodate the broader ball of the foot, while a narrower heel counter secures the back of the foot and prevents slippage.

Additionally, the materials used in the heel construction might differ between men’s and women’s versions to account for variations in where we strike our foot when we land. Women and men obviously have different centers of gravity—especially when we’re pregnant—and that changes how we strike and the wear pattern of our soles.

Brands are not just shrinking and pinking the shoes anymore. Their aim is to enhance performance and prevent running-related aches and pains. A shoe that fits properly and supports the foot’s natural movement can improve running efficiency and reduce the risk of common running-related injuries, such as blisters, plantar fasciitis, the pedi-ick black toenails, and shin splints.

Researchers have also found that, because women tend to have wider hips than men, women’s feet are more likely to strike the ground toward the outside of their shoe soles. The inward rolling of the foot, called pronation, that results from this explains why more women are believed to overpronate than men (aka, walk a bit duck-footed.). Some women’s running shoes account for this increased tendency with stability features in the sole, such as guide rails and medial posts, to provide more support.

This list includes what we regard as the best shoe in its category. But there are still plenty of other shoes for you to choose from.

For the plushest ride and more foam underfoot, check out the Best Cushioned Running Shoes.

If you’re an overpronator or think you need more support, take a look at the Best Stability Shoes.

And if you want more of a selection of non-road shoes, visit the Best Trail Shoes.

No matter the distance or your shoe preferences, there’s a great shoe for you on our lists.

What’s the size difference between men’s and women’s running shoes?

If you prefer wearing men’s running shoes, size down 1.5. For example: A women’s size 10 would equal a men’s size 8.5.

When should you change out your running shoes?

Running shoe shelf life is dependent on the runner. Some runners wear down their shoes after only a couple weeks, others have their shoes well past several months. The standard mileage on everyday trainers is 350 to 500 miles, 250 to 300 for lightweight shoes, and 100 to 250 for racing or minimalist shoes.

If you don’t keep track of mileage, a good rule of thumb is switching out shoes twice a year. For racing shoes, two to three races.

You can put your shoes in the washing machine with some detergent, set on cold. Never put your shoes in the dryer—it will melt the glue and make them degrade faster.

Instead, remove the insoles and allow them to air dry. Stuff wads of newspaper inside your shoes and leave them to sit for a couple hours so the paper can absorb the moisture.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8986. Skip the Gimmicky Bike Gifts. Our Editors Recommend These 20 Useful Picks Under $50

Useful, cyclist-approved picks that feel thoughtful without blowing your holiday budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

Admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

Here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

The Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

What started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

We were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

The small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

We look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

The Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

Dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” said Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”

Multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

The machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

If your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy Merino wool fabric is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep you dry.

Do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and new friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
